extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent prosecutors drafting patent applications (U.S. and foreign filings)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing robust patent specifications and claims that survive examination and litigation, including how to frame the problem, state the inventive concept, draft/spec interplay, claim strategy, and foreign-filing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the invention around the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest patents start with a clear statement of the technical problem and the failure mode of prior solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the reader (examiner, judge, jury) understand by paragraph 5 of the spec what was hard, what was tried, why those attempts failed, and what new insight enables the inventor's solution. Explain prior attempts and failure modes so the improvement and inventive step are evident from early in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the 'Single Sentence Inventive Concept'
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot fit the inventive concept into a single sentence, you do not yet have a clean invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force yourself to write: 'The new thing is that ____ enables ____ by ____.' Use this single-sentence test to clarify and distill the core inventive idea; lack of a concise formulation indicates the concept is not yet well-defined for claiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec first, claims second, then iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many practitioners write a complete spec, draft claims from it, then revise the spec to ensure every claim term has antecedent support and every claim element has at least three sentences of context in the spec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a comprehensive specification before or alongside claims; after drafting claims, go back and revise the spec so each claim term is grounded (antecedent support) and each claimed element is discussed in multiple sentences (recommendation: at least three sentences) to provide context and bolster written-description/enablement arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose generalizations, not just implementations
rubrics_metrics.description: For each implementation choice you made, ask 'what is the general principle here?' and 'what other choices would also work?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing embodiments, explicitly state the general principle underlying each implementation and provide at least two alternative ways to implement it. Avoid only describing a single concrete implementation; broad disclosure of alternatives supports broader claim scope and reduces enablement/written-description attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch the 'heart of the invention' trap
rubrics_metrics.description: If the spec repeatedly says 'the heart of the invention is X,' courts may construe every claim as requiring X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not single out one feature as the 'heart' or essential element of the invention in the specification. Over-emphasizing one feature risks limiting claim construction; instead present the invention holistically and avoid language that makes a particular feature appear mandatory across all claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor claim terms in defined concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: If your claim uses an unusual term, define it explicitly: 'As used herein, X means Y.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit definitions in the specification for unusual or newly-coined claim terms. Courts and examiners give weight to explicit definitions, which can guide claim construction and reduce ambiguity. Use clear 'as used herein' language when introducing definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical strong filing has 3-4 independent claims of different scope and type (method, system, apparatus, computer-readable medium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include several independent claims across claim categories (e.g., method, system/apparatus, computer-readable medium) and at different breadth levels. Treat each independent claim as an 'insurance policy'—if one path is invalidated or limited, others may survive. Vary scope to cover broad territory and valuable sub-regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle around the invention (claim scope layering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine the universe of all possible products. The invention occupies a small region. Each claim is a rectangle around some part of that region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the broadest claim to cover as much as possible without reading on prior art; draft narrower claims as smaller rectangles inside that broad rectangle to cover higher-value or fallback embodiments. Use this spatial analogy to plan claim scope, overlap, and fallback positions strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider litigation survivability
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim with 12 elements, each cited in a different prior art reference, will likely face an obviousness challenge. A claim with 6 elements where the inventive concept is concentrated in 2-3 specific elements is harder to attack with a multi-reference combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how easy it would be for an opponent to combine prior art references against your claims. Prefer concentrating the inventive concept into fewer, critical claim elements rather than spreading it thin across many elements, and design claims to reduce vulnerability to obviousness arguments based on combining multiple references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get foreign counterparts in mind early
rubrics_metrics.description: If you plan to file in Europe, draft with European requirements in mind from the start: avoid US-specific drafting tricks (Markush groupings work differently), keep the spec carefully neutral on prior art, and include problem-solution framing that EPO examiners find natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When global filing is anticipated, adapt drafting tactics to foreign offices' standards (e.g., EPO). Avoid relying on U.S.-centric drafting approaches that may be ineffective or harmful abroad (be cautious with Markush/grouping, prior-art statements, etc.). Include neutral problem-solution statements and other disclosures that harmonize with foreign prosecution practices to preserve flexibility and claim scope internationally.
